title: Chernoff concentration from inclusion-link spectral bounds
oneLine: A retained-set construction turns inclusion-link covariance control into scalar concentration, with a proposed mean-sensitive bound for variable-size samples.
abstract: This unrefereed analytic candidate derives a two-sided concentration inequality for additive statistics on fixed-size random sets from spectral bounds on every inclusion link. An extension assumes an inclusion-link covariance bound and obtains a negative-binomial moment-generating-function comparison and a mean-sensitive upper tail for arbitrary variable-size random sets, with a Poisson comparison at parameter one. The proof uses an attributed birth–death spectral-gap criterion and a retained-face construction that recovers original untilted inclusion laws. It does not claim matrix concentration, arbitrary Lipschitz concentration, a variable-rank lower tail or resolution of the separate TD-threshold question.

problem.name: Scalar lifted-vertex concentration from inclusion-link spectral bounds

keyResults: For rank d, link-walk bounds λ₂(P_A) ≤ η/r imply a two-sided additive concentration bound with exponent −ε²d/[4(1+η)].
The proposed covariance-based extension gives a mean-sensitive upper tail for bounded additive statistics on variable-size random sets.
A negative-binomial MGF comparison has a Poisson limit at covariance parameter one; it is not a distributional identity.
The retained-face construction recovers original inclusion-link laws and uses an explicitly attributed auxiliary spectral-gap criterion.
evidence: Written analytic proof with coordinated internal checking; supplied audit replay on 205 laws and original extension diagnostics on 100 laws and 1161 thinned links. Finite tests are not universal proof.

narration:
Concentration without independent choices. An Evidence Press briefing.

Suppose a random sample contains choices that influence one another. How unlikely is a total much larger than its average? For independent choices, concentration inequalities answer that question. Dependence makes it harder.

This candidate studies a particular way to control dependence. Imagine learning that several elements are present in the sample. The assumption limits the covariance that remains, after every such piece of information.

The original theorem uses this local condition to bound deviations of a weighted total in a fixed-size sample. A proposed extension allows the sample size to vary and makes the upper-tail bound depend on the total's expected value. A small expected count can then give a more informative bound.

The key move is to create an intermediate set. First, favour samples with larger totals. Then keep each selected element with a carefully chosen probability. Conditional on the retained set, the remainder follows an original inclusion-conditioned distribution. The proof can therefore use the assumptions it actually has, without demanding that they survive arbitrary changes of weights.

An existing birth-and-death-chain result supplies part of the argument. The paper credits it explicitly. Its proposed extension compares a moment-generating function with a negative-binomial form, reducing to a Poisson comparison at one parameter value. That does not say the total has either distribution.

The scope matters. These are scalar, additive statistics. The paper does not establish a matrix theorem, a result for every Lipschitz function, or a variable-size lower-tail bound. Computational checks are diagnostics, not a universal proof.

The revised proof and finite checks have been examined internally. The manuscript also gives an example showing why a comparable lower-tail statement needs more assumptions when sample size varies. The paper and code are linked on Evidence Press. This is an unrefereed candidate dated the thirteenth of October, twenty twenty-six. The narration uses a synthetic British voice and is not additional scientific evidence.
